newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - US Office sees more consolidation.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - US Office sees more consolidation.

text.p: Whether the proposed merger of Staples Inc and Office Depot Inc goes through or not, at least one of their competitors said Thursday he sees consolidation sweeping the office products industry in 1997.
"I see a fundamental shift," said Jonathan Ledecky, chairman of U.S. Office Products Co, in an interview. "I'm either going to be the main entree for dinner, or I'm going to be making reservations."
Several smaller office-products companies already have contacted U.S. Office Products about possible alliances, he said.
Ledecky said U.S. Office Products was well-positioned to benefit from the trend, "either as an acquisition vehicle, or to be acquired."

U.S. Office Products shares fell almost 2 points to 31-5/8 on Thursday after the company released third quarter financial results showing net income of $0.20 per share, down from $0.33 for the same period a year ago.
Excluding non-recurring charges from acquisitions, the company's net income per share was $0.30, compared to analysts' estimates of $0.28 to $0.29, Ledecky said.

He said the Washington-based company's growth has been based on acquisitions, a trend that will sweep the industry no matter what the U.S. Federal Trade Commission decides regarding the Staples-Office Depot merger.
"The world changes on March 5" when the FTC makes its decision, Ledecky said. "I see monumental repercussions."
The Federal Trade Commission this week set an unusual Saturday session to consider the merger. Staples and Office Depot both delayed special stockholders' meetings from Thursday until March 7.

If the industry's two biggest players merge to form a company with annual sales in the $10 billion range, companies such as U.S. Office Products in the next tier down would feel pressed to seek similar purchasing efficiencies, Ledecky said.
Even if the merger of giants does not go through, vertical mergers with smaller companies would be a logical step for the industry, he said.
